title: When is Warmstarting Effective for Scaling Language Models?
claim: Warmstarting variants rank consistently by convergence speed, but only the best one matches or beats scratch training at every target scale.
layout: 4 line-plot panels in a row, shared legend below, growth ratio titles
description: A row of four line plots shows validation loss against FLOPs for growing a model from a smaller base: width 64 to 128, 64 to 256, 128 to 512, and 256 to 768. Each panel has a horizontal black dash-dot line for the base model's final loss and a thick gray curve for training from scratch. Warmstart variants are drawn in blue for Zeros and Clone, pale gray and salmon for the +Perturb versions, crimson for Shrink+Clone+Perturb, and bold orange for Shrink+Zeros+Perturb (SZP). Orange drops fastest and tracks or beats the gray scratch curve. The blue curves plateau high. One shared legend sits under all panels. The eye goes first to the orange curve against the gray one.
caption: Comparing the simplest set of realizations of Equation (2), for different target scale runs, given the base checkpoint (base →target); Zeros and Clone represent the choices for G, the growth function; Zeros+/Clone+Perturb represents the addition of noise to the grown matrix; Adding Shrink to the inherited base model implies a scalar multiplication of λshrink to the base matrix before any growth operation is applied. For either choice of G, Shrink+G+Perturb converges faster than G+Perturb, which converges faster than G alone. Scratch runs the target model with standard initialisation (no warmstarting), while Base marks the final loss of the smaller base model used for WS. All WS models appear to recover and go past the Base loss quickly; only SZP keeps a convergence rate better or matched with the vanilla run from Scratch.
abstract: Model growth from a given checkpoint aims to accelerate training of a larger model, offering potential resource savings. Despite recent interest, warmstarting has seen limited practical adoption in large-scale training. We attribute this to two underexplored factors: (1) an overemphasis on preserving the smaller model's performance at initialization, which constrains operator design for new architectures, and (2) insufficient analysis of how growth interacts with hyperparameters and scaling behavior, compounded by inconsistent growth factors across the literature. We show that preserving the base model's initial post-growth performance is not necessary for strong final performance, and that simple, architecture-agnostic growth strategies can outperform more complex warmstarting operators. Crucially, we empirically identify an upper bound on the growth factor $g$ beyond which training from scratch is more efficient. We observe this across multiple ablation setups. Notably, this limit is also present, but unreported, in prior published results. Across our experiments on dense MLPs and dense language models, we find that a $2\times$ growth factor is the most reliable in yielding convergence speedups, with gains most pronounced under 20 tokens/parameter budgets and diminishing as budget increases. We fit scaling laws over these observations to provide predictive guidance for practitioners deciding when and how much to grow. Together, our analysis provides practical guidelines and empirical limits for model growth.
